title: Maternal sepsis
blurb: Grade suspected sepsis in pregnant and recently pregnant women with NICE NG255, act within the 1-hour targets and transfer safely from the community.
question: Five days after a caesarean birth, Hannah is visited at home by her community midwife. She feels very unwell, her respiratory rate is 26 per minute and her wound is red and oozing. What should the midwife do?

teach.body: Formally (NICE NG255): sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection. In plain English: the body's reaction to an infection starts damaging its own organs. In pregnancy and after birth it can look non-specific: she may just feel very unwell and may not have a temperature (1.1.2). The midwife's first job is to think 'could this be sepsis?' whenever there are signs of infection (1.1.1).

items: Anyone pregnant, or who has given birth, had a termination or a miscarriage in the past 6 weeks.
Especially: impaired immunity, diabetes or gestational diabetes, or other comorbidities.
Invasive procedures such as caesarean, forceps birth or removal of retained products.
Prolonged rupture of membranes; close contact with group A streptococcal infection (for example scarlet fever).
Continued vaginal bleeding or an offensive vaginal discharge.

teach.caption: Baseline heart rate in pregnancy is 10 to 15 beats per minute higher (1.4.4). Pulse oximeters may overestimate saturation in people with darker skin (1.4.9).
1.6.1-1.6.6. If a definite diagnosis cannot be made or care cannot be given safely at home, refer urgently for emergency care.

teach.h: In hospital: one or more high risk criteria (NG255 1.7.2-1.7.9)

steps.label: Senior review now
steps.sub: Senior clinical decision maker assesses immediately

steps.label: Venous bloods
steps.sub: Gas with lactate and glucose, cultures, FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting

steps.label: Fluids by lactate
steps.sub: Bolus within 1 hour if lactate over 2 or systolic 90 or less

steps.label: Monitor and escalate
steps.sub: At least every 30 min; consultant if no response in 1 hour

teach.h: Lactate and fluids for high risk women
head: Finding
Action
rows: Lactate over 4 or systolic 90 or less
Bolus within 1 hour; refer to critical care
teach.caption: NG255 1.7.4-1.7.6, 1.9.2. Reassess after each bolus; oxygen target 94-98% (1.10.1).

teach.h: Moderate to high risk in hospital
teach.body: Two or more moderate to high risk criteria, or a systolic of 91 to 100: venous bloods including lactate and a clinician review within 1 hour. If lactate is over 2 or there is acute kidney injury, treat as high risk. If not, repeat the structured assessment at least hourly and have a senior decision maker review the need for antibiotics within 3 hours. One criterion alone: clinician review within 1 hour (1.7.10-1.7.13).

teach.h: Scenario: Hannah at home, day 5 after caesarean
items: The midwife thinks 'could this be sepsis?': recent caesarean (invasive procedure) and a red, oozing wound.
Respiratory rate 26 is a high risk criterion. Heart rate 124 and feeling very unwell add to the picture.
She calls 999 for emergency transfer and pre-alerts the receiving hospital (1.6.1-1.6.2).
She hands over clearly with SBAR and records her findings and the times.
Hannah's baby also needs assessment for infection, as puerperal sepsis is suspected (NG194 1.2.8).

teach.text: A normal temperature does not rule out sepsis (NG255 1.1.2). In table 1, a LOW tympanic temperature (under 36°C) is the moderate to high risk criterion; fever is not on the table at all.

items: High-risk group: pregnant, or within 6 weeks of birth, termination or miscarriage.
High risk criteria include RR 25+, systolic 90 or less, HR over 130, no urine for 18 hours, mottled or ashen skin.
Community: any high risk criterion means 999 transfer with a pre-alert.
Hospital: senior review now, bloods with lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.
Fluids guided by lactate; 500 mL crystalloid over under 15 minutes, then reassess.

summary: You can now grade suspected sepsis in pregnant and recently pregnant women using NG255 table 1 and decide when a woman at home needs 999 transfer. You can also describe the 1-hour hospital actions, lactate-guided fluids and the escalation pathway.

A.q: According to NICE NG255, for how long after giving birth is a woman considered part of the high-risk group for sepsis?
A.why: NG255 1.2.1: people who are pregnant, or who have given birth or had a termination or miscarriage in the past 6 weeks, are in a high risk group for sepsis.

whyNot.1: 28 days (4 weeks) is how long NG255 counts someone as 'recently pregnant' after birth; the high-risk group in 1.2.1 runs for 6 weeks.
whyNot.2: 12 weeks relates to the definition of secondary PPH, not the NG255 sepsis risk group.
whyNot.3: 10 days is far shorter than the 6 weeks in NG255 1.2.1.

A.q: A woman 3 days after birth has suspected sepsis. Which finding is a high risk criterion in NICE NG255 table 1?
options: Heart rate of 115 beats per minute
A.why: A systolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg or less is a high risk criterion in NG255 table 1.

whyNot.0: A respiratory rate of 21 to 24 is moderate to high risk; high risk starts at 25.
whyNot.1: A heart rate of 100 to 130 is moderate to high risk; high risk is more than 130.
whyNot.3: A tympanic temperature under 36°C is a moderate to high risk criterion, not high risk.

A.q: A woman on the postnatal ward meets a high risk criterion for sepsis. Within what time should broad-spectrum antibiotics be given?
A.why: NG255 1.7.2: give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial without delay, within 1 hour of identifying that she meets any high risk criterion.

whyNot.0: 3 hours is the senior review window for 2 or more moderate to high criteria with lactate 2 or lower, not for high risk.
whyNot.1: 4 hours is too long; the NG255 target for high risk is 1 hour.
whyNot.2: NG255 sets 1 hour as the target; 30 minutes is the minimum monitoring frequency for high risk.

B.q: A community midwife visits Leah, 10 days after a forceps birth. She is confused and has mottled skin. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask her GP to visit later today
Take a vaginal swab and await results
B.why: New altered mental state and mottled skin are high risk criteria. Outside hospital this needs emergency transfer, usually 999, with a pre-alert (NG255 1.6.1-1.6.2).

whyNot.0: A delayed GP visit is not appropriate when high risk criteria are present; she needs emergency care now.
whyNot.2: Masking fever and delaying review risks deterioration and death.
whyNot.3: Swabs help find the source but must not delay emergency transfer.

B.q: A woman with suspected sepsis meets a high risk criterion. Her venous lactate is 3.1 mmol/L and systolic BP 104 mmHg. What does NICE advise about IV fluids?
options: Give a fluid bolus within 1 hour
Consider a bolus if BP falls
Restrict fluids to 80 mL per hour
Wait for the full blood count
B.why: NG255 1.7.5: with any high risk criterion and lactate between 2 and 4 mmol/L, give an IV fluid bolus without delay (within 1 hour).

whyNot.1: 'Consider' applies when lactate is below 2; at 2 to 4 a bolus is given.
whyNot.2: The 80 mL per hour limit applies to severe pre-eclampsia, not sepsis.
whyNot.3: Fluid resuscitation is not delayed for routine blood results.

B.q: For a woman aged 16 or over with suspected sepsis who needs fluid resuscitation, what bolus does NICE recommend?
B.why: NG255 1.9.2: 500 mL of crystalloid containing sodium 130-154 mmol/L over less than 15 minutes, then reassess.

whyNot.0: NICE recommends crystalloid, and a bolus is given in under 15 minutes, not over an hour.
whyNot.1: Glucose 5% is not a resuscitation fluid; the bolus must contain sodium 130-154 mmol/L.
whyNot.3: This is not the NG255 adult bolus and is far too slow to be a resuscitation bolus.

C.q: On the postnatal ward, Zainab has a heart rate of 118 and respiratory rate of 23. Her lactate is 1.6 mmol/L and kidney function is normal. No cause is found. What is the next step?
options: Treat as high risk and give antibiotics now
Hourly reassessment and senior review within 3 hours
C.why: Two moderate to high risk criteria with lactate 2 or lower, no AKI and no definite diagnosis: repeat structured assessment at least hourly and senior review of the need for antibiotics within 3 hours (NG255 1.7.12).

whyNot.0: She would be treated as high risk if lactate were over 2 or she had AKI; neither applies.
whyNot.1: With two moderate to high risk criteria she needs ongoing hospital assessment, not discharge.
whyNot.3: Critical care referral is for high risk women with lactate over 4 or systolic 90 or less.

C.q: A woman meeting high risk sepsis criteria has had antibiotics and two fluid boluses but remains hypotensive 1 hour later. Who should now be alerted?
options: The consultant, to attend in person
The ward manager, to arrange staffing
C.why: NG255 1.7.9 and 1.9.4: alert a consultant to attend in person if a high risk woman does not respond within 1 hour of an intervention or after a second bolus.

whyNot.0: Microbiology advice may help with antibiotics but does not provide the urgent senior bedside review needed.
whyNot.2: Primary care follow-up is not the escalation for a deteriorating inpatient.
whyNot.3: Staffing support does not replace consultant review of a woman not responding to treatment.

C.q: A midwife suspects puerperal sepsis in a woman on day 2 after birth whose baby is rooming in with her. What else should the midwife arrange?
options: Move the baby to the nursery
Assess the baby for signs of infection
C.why: If puerperal sepsis is suspected in the woman, assess the baby for infection (NG194 1.2.8). Maternal sepsis is also a risk factor for early-onset neonatal infection (NG195).

whyNot.0: Separating the baby is not recommended; the baby needs assessment, not removal.
whyNot.1: There is no NICE advice to stop breastfeeding because of maternal sepsis.
whyNot.2: Antibiotics for the baby are decided by a clinician after assessment using the NG195 framework.

reteach.title: Two traffic lights, one clock
reteach.question: Think of NG255 as two traffic lights (high risk is red, moderate to high is amber) and one clock that starts the moment a red light shows. What happens when the light turns red?

blocks.body: One high risk finding (for example respiratory rate 25 or more, systolic 90 or less, heart rate over 130, new confusion, mottled skin) is enough. At home: 999 and a pre-alert. In hospital: a senior doctor now, bloods with lactate, and antibiotics and any needed fluid bolus within 1 hour. Amber findings need a clinician within 1 hour; with two or more, a venous lactate (and kidney function) decides whether the light is really red.

blocks.text: Two amber criteria plus lactate over 2, or acute kidney injury, are treated as red (NG255 1.7.11).

explain.body: Think 'could this be sepsis?' with any sign of infection. Presentations can be vague and afebrile. Listen to concerns from the woman and her family, and consider an early warning score in any setting (NG255 1.1.1-1.1.8).

test.q: A woman 4 days after birth says she feels 'really unwell' but her temperature is 37.0°C. What is the best interpretation?
options: Sepsis is unlikely without a fever
Sepsis is still possible and needs assessment
test.why: People with sepsis may have non-specific presentations, such as feeling very unwell, and may not have a high temperature (NG255 1.1.2).

whyNot.0: NICE warns that sepsis may present without a high temperature.
whyNot.2: Feeling very unwell is a recognised non-specific presentation and needs structured assessment.
whyNot.3: Waiting a day risks missing rapid deterioration; she needs assessment now.

explain.body: High risk: new altered mental state, RR 25+, new oxygen need, systolic 90 or less, HR over 130, no urine 18 hours, mottled or ashen skin, cyanosis, non-blanching rash. Moderate to high: RR 21-24, systolic 91-100, HR 100-130, no urine 12-18 hours, temperature under 36°C, wound infection signs.

test.q: Which finding in a recently pregnant woman with suspected sepsis is a moderate to high risk criterion rather than a high risk criterion?
options: No urine for the past 19 hours
Heart rate of 136 beats per minute
Redness and discharge at her wound
test.why: Signs of potential infection at a surgical site (redness, swelling, discharge or wound breakdown) are a moderate to high risk criterion in NG255 table 1.

whyNot.0: A non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash is a high risk criterion.
whyNot.1: No urine for 18 hours or more is a high risk criterion.
whyNot.2: A heart rate over 130 is a high risk criterion.

explain.body: Outside hospital, any high risk criterion means referral for emergency care, usually by 999 ambulance, with a pre-alert to secondary care and immediate transfer (NG255 1.6.1-1.6.2). Moderate to high risk: assess for a definitive diagnosis and whether she can be treated safely at home; if not, refer urgently (1.6.5).

explain.h: At home with a high risk criterion

test.q: At a home visit, a woman 2 weeks after a caesarean has a systolic BP of 86 mmHg and a heart rate of 134. What should the midwife do first?
options: Arrange a GP appointment for tomorrow
Ask her to attend triage by taxi
Take bloods and send them to the lab
test.why: Systolic 90 or less and HR over 130 are high risk criteria; outside hospital she needs emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert (NG255 1.6.1-1.6.2).

whyNot.0: A next-day appointment is a dangerous delay for a woman meeting high risk criteria.
whyNot.1: NICE advises the most appropriate means of transport, usually a 999 ambulance, for high risk criteria.
whyNot.3: Community bloods would delay the emergency treatment she needs in hospital.

explain.body: For one or more high risk criteria: senior clinical decision maker assesses immediately; venous blood gas with lactate and glucose, cultures and other bloods; broad-spectrum antimicrobial within 1 hour; fluids guided by lactate; monitoring continuously or at least every 30 minutes (NG255 1.7.2-1.7.7).

test.q: A woman on the labour ward meets high risk sepsis criteria. How often, at a minimum, should she be monitored?
test.why: NG255 1.7.7: monitor continuously or a minimum of once every 30 minutes, using physiological track and trigger systems.

whyNot.1: Hourly reassessment applies to 2 or more moderate to high criteria with lactate 2 or lower, not high risk.
whyNot.2: Every 2 hours is far less often than NICE recommends for high risk.
whyNot.3: 4-hourly observations are routine labour observations, not sepsis monitoring.
